questions.question: State Lambert's law.
questions.solution_html:
• Source: Provides stable, intense radiation across desired wavelengths (e.g.
  • deuterium lamp for UV, Nernst glower for IR).
  • Monochromator: Disperses polychromatic light into individual wavelengths using
  • grating/prism.
  • Detector: Converts light signal into electrical output proportional to intensity
  • (photodiode, PMT).
  • → Together they enable accurate measurement of absorbance and transmittance.
  • (1 mark each = 3)

questions.question: Discuss the contribution of detectors in improving chromatographic analysis in forensic investigations.
questions.solution_html:
• Detectors transform the separated components into measurable signals, increasing
  • sensitivity and precision. Types and contributions: UV–Vis Detector: Measures
  • absorbance of eluted species. Fluorescence Detector: Enhances selectivity for
  • fluorescent compounds. Refractive Index Detector: Universal but less sensitive.
  • Electron Capture Detector (GC): Highly sensitive for halogenated compounds. Mass
  • spectrometric Detector: Provides molecular identity and quantitation. Detectors allow
  • trace-level analysis in forensic samples like drugs, inks, and toxicants. (Definition–1;
  • Types–3; Forensic importance–2)

questions.question: Explain the width of absorption lines and their role in interpretation of NMR?
questions.solution_html:
• Line width depends on magnetic field homogeneity and relaxation time (T ). Broader
  • lines: short relaxation, less resolution. Narrow lines: better separation of chemical
  • shifts and coupling. Inter-nuclear interactions and viscosity also affect width.
  • Understanding line width aids in accurate chemical shift and multiplet analysis for
  • structural elucidation. (Definition–2; Factors–2; Importance–2)
